newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SANLAM SEES S.AFRICAN INTEREST RATES DOWN 3PCT.
newsitem.headline: SANLAM SEES S.AFRICAN INTEREST RATES DOWN 3PCT.

text.p: Sanlam Asset Management chief economist Jac Laubscher said on Friday he expected the first of three bank rate cuts in September to stimulate South Africa's recovery from an anticipated six-month recession.

"We remain of the opinion that we could see two cuts of 100 basis points each in the bank rate this year, one in the third quarter and another in the fourth quarter," he said in an economic review released on Friday.
"Our view of how the business cycle will proceed into 1998 and beyond leads us to believe that we will see one further reduction in the bank rate in the first quarter of 1998."
South Africa reported negative economic growth in the first quarter of 1997 and Laubscher said in an interview coinciding with the release of his report:
"There is a very real possibility that the second quarter figure will also be negative and then, technically, we're in a recession."
He said he expected economic growth to fall from 3.1 percent in 1996 to 1.7 percent in calendar 1997 before picking up in 1998 for annual growth equivalent to three percent of GDP.
"The single most important development the markets are waiting for in order to gain new momentum is the first cut in the bank rate," he said.

He added in the interview that Reserve Bank governor Chris Stals could delay the recovery if he postponed beyond September the widely anticipated first cut in the key discount rate from the 17 percent level set last November.

He said Stals needed urgently to bring monetary policy in line with the business cycle by trimming the real interest rate created by high central bank rates in an environment of sustained single-digit inflation.

"We have a window of opportunity that is probably not going to remain open for more than the next six to 12 months. During this period, inflation will be in a declining trend and the global interest rate environment will be fairly neutral.
"Should we therefore miss the opportunity to lower the bank rate meaningfully -- by say three percent -- in the next six to 12 months, it will become very difficult to do so," he said.
Laubscher said he expected inflation to fall from the 9.5 percent year-on-year figure recorded in May to a low of between 6.5 and seven percent in the second quarter of 1998.
The anticipated economic recovery would renew pressure on consumer prices around this point and limit the central bank's ability to relax its tight monetary policy.
Laubscher said he expected the real effective exchange rate of the South African rand to remain stable, ending the year between 4.50 rand and 4.60 rand to the dollar.
"In our view, the lower turning point in the business cycle will be reached in the second half of 1997 and business conditions will start to improve, resulting in an acceleration in earnings growth."
As economic growth accelerates next year, however, a weaking current account of the balance of payments, with the deficit peaking around nine billion rand, could put the rand under renewed pressure.
